1:
Ambrose sets the scene from what went before: after many cures of many kinds, the crowd had stopped caring about time or place. Evening came and they followed; a lake stood in the way and they still pressed on. Chrysostom explains the pressing as affection rather than need: they clung to him with love and admiration and wanted to keep him; who would go away while such things were being done? And it was not the miracles alone, Chrysostom adds, since his whole appearance overflowed with grace, which is why they listened in silence and never broke the chain of his discourse.

Where this episode belongs in the story is a real question, and two of the witnesses face it. Henry places it before the two miracles that closed the previous chapter and identifies it with the brief accounts of the calling of Peter and Andrew in the other Gospels, explaining that those writers had the calling in view and not the draught of fishes, while Luke records it among the many signs done before the disciples that the earlier books had left unwritten. Robertson agrees that Luke has departed from his usual practice of following Mark's order, and holds that the renewed call of the four fishermen came before the first tour of Galilee, so that Luke is telling in his own way the incident the other two had already given.

The lake's three names are sorted out by Bede. It is the sea of Galilee from the province beside it and the sea of Tiberias from a neighbouring city, but Gennesaret is a name taken from the nature of the water itself, which is thought to raise a breeze on itself by the crossing of its waves — the Greek, he says, meaning something like making a breeze for itself — since the water is never steady. Calvin works the philology from the Hebrew side, tracing the name to an adjoining city in the older history and noting that the form was altered as the language became corrupted. Barnes simply reports that Gennesaret was the more ancient of the names.

The boats are deflated by everyone who touches them. Clarke objects outright to calling them ships: they were small craft for working nets off a flat beach, one end of the net made fast ashore while the men rowed out paying it into a half-circle and came back with the rope of the other end. Barnes agrees they were open boats without decks, light enough to be hauled up on the sand, and cites Josephus for two hundred and thirty of them on that lake with four or five men to each. Gill assigns the two — one to Peter and Andrew, the other to Zebedee and his sons.

Bede then reads the same two boats as a figure: they stand for the circumcision and the uncircumcision, and the Lord sees both because he knows his own in either people. The fishermen on his account are the doctors of the Church, who take men in the net of faith and bring them ashore to the land of the living; and the nets that are now spread and now washed and folded mark that not every season is fit for teaching, some being given to speech and some to the teacher's own discipline.

Lightfoot supplies the custom that made the scene unremarkable and then the rule that made it irregular. Teaching outside the synagogue and the house of study was ordinary — one rabbi taught a whole day in the street before the temple mount, another in the streets of Tiberias — and yet a later authority forbade it: doctors were not to teach their disciples in the streets, and he rebuked a colleague for teaching his brothers' sons there.
3:
Why he taught from a boat at all is answered practically. Clarke says the crowd pressed so hard that he could not conveniently speak, and notes that the smooth still water would have carried the sound admirably to those on the beach. Barnes works the acoustics further: the place was probably a small cove, so that once he had pushed off the people stood round him as in an amphitheatre, the lake unruffled and nothing on the shore to interrupt. He adds that sitting was the ordinary posture of a Jewish teacher, and cannot resist the scene itself — the Son of God preaching from the bosom of a placid lake, which Barnes calls an emblem of the peaceful influence of his own doctrine, to the poor crowd on the sand. Ellicott adds that this appears to have been a method he used more than once. Robertson notes that the verb for putting out is a rare double compound, found in Xenophon and later writers but only twice in the New Testament, and used in the other place for going back.

Cyril reads the sequence as a deliberate turn: having taught the people sufficiently, the Lord returns to his mighty works, and goes fishing for his disciples by way of their own trade. Chrysostom states the principle behind that — in his condescension he called the wise men by a star and the fishermen by their fishing. Cyril adds what the loan of the boat earned its owner: the Lord did not leave the master of the ship unrewarded, but did him a double kindness, the multitude of fishes and then the making of him a disciple.

What Peter already knew about the man giving the order divides the witnesses flatly. Gill takes the title Peter uses to mean he already knew him for the Messiah, the king of Israel, a teacher sent from God. Barnes says the opposite: Peter knew little of Jesus then and was not yet a chosen apostle, and Jesus came to these fishermen almost a stranger and unknown — which is what makes the obedience a remarkable instance of faith, nothing being less likely than a catch after a whole night of failure.

The title itself is unusual enough that Barnes and Clarke both stop on it. This is its first occurrence in the New Testament, and Luke alone uses it, where the other evangelists write Rabbi or Lord; the word means a prefect, one set over others or over affairs, and so comes to mean an instructor. Clarke thinks Peter intends both senses at once, listening to him as a teacher of divine doctrine and obeying him as one with authority to command. Lightfoot supplies the idiom behind the complaint, noting that toiling all night is the phrase the rabbinic schools used for labour that runs through the night, as they spoke of labouring all the day.

Cyril describes the haul itself in its confusion: they took so many that they could not draw them in, and had to call the other boat, and Peter could only beckon, being unable to speak for astonishment. Augustine uses the broken nets to separate this miracle from the one that looks like it. The other took place after the resurrection and at a different season, the nets were let down on the right side, and a hundred and fifty-three large fishes were counted — a number the evangelist had to record, because the point there was that the nets held despite the size. Here the nets break, and Augustine takes the contrast to be deliberate.

Ambrose reads the two accounts of Peter's boat as one figure with two halves. In one Gospel the ship is beaten about by the waves; in this one it is filled with fishes; so that the Church may be understood as first wavering and at last abounding.
6:
Whether the nets actually tore is a clean disagreement, and it turns on a tense. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott all read the verb as inchoative or imperfect: the nets began to break, or were breaking, and Barnes points out that if they had really given way the fish would have escaped and there would have been no miracle to report. Clarke supports the reading with a grammarians' rule — that verbs signifying the accomplishment of a thing are often to be understood of the beginning of it — and cites examples collected out of Herodotus. Robertson takes the opposite view and says so plainly: the nets were actually tearing in two, and on that account the men stood to lose the whole catch, which is why the second boat had to be called at once.

Gill identifies the partners as Zebedee and his sons, and explains the beckoning by distance: they had probably not put out but lay at anchor near the shore, out of earshot, so that signs had to serve. Barnes agrees they were too far off to be easily heard, and then borrows from a modern traveller a whole page on how such fishing was done — the hand-net, the drag-net, and the bag or basket nets of every conceivable size that are worked so as to enclose fish out in deep water, one of which he supposes Simon had been using. The same writer describes the night fishing that Peter refers to: the boat gliding over a flashing sea with a blazing torch, the men staring into the water until the prey is sighted and then flinging net or spear, and the tired crews coming sullenly into harbour in the morning having toiled all night for nothing. Every kind of fishing, the account concludes, is uncertain — a dozen times the net closes on nothing, and then every throw is successful for no visible reason.

Calvin states what the miracle was for. Its design was to make Christ's divinity known and so to draw Peter and the others into discipleship; and the general lesson he takes from it is that we have no reason to fear our labour will go unblessed when it is undertaken on Christ's authority and under his guidance. It was the divine glory shown in the miracle, Calvin says, that made his authority fully acknowledged.

Peter's recoil is explained by two of the older readers in quite different registers. Bede puts it as a proportion: Peter was astonished at the divine gift, and the more he feared the less he now presumed. Cyril gives it a legal cause. Recalling the crimes he had committed, Peter is alarmed and trembles, and believes that being unclean he cannot possibly receive one who is clean — for he had learnt from the law to distinguish what is defiled from what is holy, and applied the rule to himself.

Augustine notices an absence rather than a presence. Andrew is not named here, though he is thought to have been in that boat on the strength of the other two accounts, which name him.

Ambrose turns Peter's words into an instruction for the reader. Say it yourself, he urges — depart from me, for I am a sinful man — so that God may answer, fear not; confess the sin and the Lord will pardon it. What follows is what Ambrose finds most remarkable in the whole exchange: the goodness of a Lord who gives men so much that they are put in a position to make others alive.
9:
The astonishment is rendered more physically than the English suggests. Ellicott gives it as astonishment seizing him; Robertson makes the Greek say that a wonder held him round, and notes that it held not only Peter but everyone with him. Gill fills the boat out with Andrew and the hired men, and reminds the reader that James and John had come across from the other boat and so witnessed the whole thing. Ellicott catches a distinction the translation loses: the word for partners here is not the one used earlier, that meaning sharers in a particular piece of work and this a standing partnership in business.

The promise made to Peter turns on a single verb, and three of the commentators independently stop on it. Clarke renders it thou shalt catch men alive, and says that is the proper force of the word: the discoveries of God tend to life and not to death, and where these fish are taken to be killed and eaten, those converted under such a ministry are taken to be preserved to eternal life. Ellicott adds that this is Luke's equivalent for the fishers of men in the other two Gospels, and that the verb occurs only once more in the New Testament. Robertson notes the periphrastic future, which stresses the continuing action, and confirms that the old verb means to take alive.

What the promise meant for Peter in particular is Bede's concern. He takes it as especially Peter's own, the Lord explaining to him what the taking of fish had signified — that as he now takes fish with a net, so afterwards he will take men with words; and Bede reads the whole order of the event as a picture of what goes on daily in the Church, of which Peter is the type.

Tertullian asks the question none of the others asks: out of all the trades available, why should this one have been singled out to furnish apostles? His answer is that the choice was itself the point. In saying that Peter would henceforth catch men, the Lord was showing them the meaning of a prophecy already fulfilled — it was he who had said by Jeremiah that he would send many fishers, and that they should fish them, meaning men. Tertullian's reading explains the response as well as the call: they left their boats then and there because they understood that the speaker had begun to do what he had long ago declared.

What the leaving cost is weighed two ways. Barnes is careful not to overstate it — a couple of small boats and some nets were not much — and then presses the point that it was everything they had, their whole living, so that the act proved their love as truly as if palaces and gold had been given up. Chrysostom looks at the timing: they were in the middle of the best fishing of their lives when the command came, and did not delay; and he takes that for the measure of the obedience Christ asks, not to be deferred even when some pressing necessity seems to excuse it. Clarke turns the episode into a method, noting three steps in order — he teaches in their hearing, so that they may know his doctrine; he works a miracle before their eyes, so that they may be convinced of his power; and only then does he call them to go out with that doctrine and in that power.

Ellicott closes on the difficulty the words create for harmonising the Gospels. That they forsook all is the strongest single argument for treating this as the same occasion the other evangelists describe; but he points out that it can be reconciled with a separate earlier call by supposing a temporary return to their old trade, of the kind that happened once after the resurrection.
12:
Where this happened is left vague by the text and filled in three ways. Gill guesses Capernaum, or somewhere hard by it; Clarke prefers a Galilean town, naming Chorazin or Bethsaida as likely. Ambrose takes the vagueness for the point: no definite place is named, he says, precisely to signify that it was not one people of one city but all nations that were healed. He also counts the miracle in sequence — the fourth since Jesus came to Capernaum — and draws a conclusion from the number, that as the fourth day was the one God lit with the sun and made more glorious than the rest, this work should be reckoned more glorious than those before it.

How bad the case was is where Luke's own hand shows. Robertson points out that where the other two Gospels say simply a leper, Luke writes full of leprosy, evidently a case far advanced and covered with sores, which he takes as the physician's observation; and he notes the curious provision of the law, which treated the most advanced cases as less unclean than the earlier stages. Gill supplies the clinical picture from the old physicians — a hoarse voice that comes through the nose rather than the mouth, and blood full of little white shining bodies. Robertson adds a smaller difference of report, that here the man falls on his face where the parallel has him kneeling.

Bede uses the healing and the withdrawal that follows it to state a doctrine precisely. The retiring to pray is not to be ascribed to the nature that says I will, be thou clean, but to the nature that put out a hand and touched a leper; and he guards the distinction against the obvious misreading — not that there is a double person of the Son, as Nestorius held, but that in one and the same person, as there are two natures, so there are two operations.

Why the man was sent to the priest is answered three ways, and the three do not quite agree. Chrysostom makes it pastoral: men often remember God while they are sick and grow dull once they recover, so the Lord binds this man to keep God before his eyes, and sends him to be inspected and by the priest's own sanction reckoned clean. Ambrose makes it evidential, and turns it on the priest rather than the patient — the priest was to learn that the cure had come not by the order of the law but by a grace above the law; and since the sacrifice was commanded by Moses, the Lord shows in requiring it that he does not abrogate the law but fulfils it. Augustine is more careful still, noting that the Lord appears here to approve a sacrifice which the Church does not require, and suggesting the command is to be understood of a moment when the older order had not yet been superseded.

Clarke supplies a parallel from outside scripture altogether: a Hindu recovering from sickness presents the offerings vowed in his distress, a goat or sweetmeats or milk, whatever the sacred books direct — all nations, he observes, have agreed in this kind of gratitude-offering for benefits received from the object of their worship.

Robertson closes on a point of style. The charge to tell no one begins as an indirect command after the verb of charging and then slips into direct quotation, which he notes is an ordinary Greek idiom and a frequent habit of Luke's in particular. Gill, for his part, is content to say what the man was charged to keep quiet about: the cure, and the one from whom he had received it.
15:
The silence commanded produced the opposite of silence, and Gill states the irony without softening it: the more he was charged to say nothing, the more the man blazed it abroad, being elated with his cure and full of gratitude to his benefactor. Ellicott notes that Luke's report here agrees with Mark, where the parallel account closes at the command itself, and that both the verbs — the fame going out and the crowds coming together — stand in the tense of continuous action. Robertson makes the same grammatical point and draws the consequence: the fame of Jesus kept going, and the further the report spread the more the crowds came.

The withdrawal that follows is read by Clarke as a habit rather than an incident. The Greek, he argues, is better given as he frequently withdrew into the desert, a settled custom rather than one occasion; and he turns it into a charge to ministers, who must get fresh supplies of light and power from God by prayer, since a man can give nothing he has not first received. Gill puts the same withdrawal more simply, as rest from the fatigue of preaching and healing and an opportunity for private prayer away from company.

Gregory Nazianzen presses the oddity of it. The works were done among the people, but the praying was done for the most part in the wilderness — which, he says, sanctions the liberty of resting a while from labour in order to hold converse with God with a pure heart. He is careful about why: not that the Lord needed any change or retirement, there being nothing in him to be relaxed and no place that could contain him, but so that we might know plainly that there is a time for action and a time for every higher occupation.

Henry takes the setting of the next scene as instructive in two small ways. It was not the sabbath — Luke would have said so — but an ordinary weekday, and Henry argues from it that preaching and hearing the word are good works on any day if done well, the command to labour six days covering the soul's business as well as the world's. Nor was it the synagogue but a private house; and even in the place where we ordinarily talk with our friends, he says, it is not improper to give and receive good instruction. Barnes and Clarke both identify the house as being at Capernaum.

The clause about the power being present to heal draws two very different kinds of attention. Cyril takes it doctrinally and rules out the natural misreading: the Lord was not borrowing another's power, but healing as God by a power inherent in himself. He contrasts the ordinary case, in which men are made worthy of spiritual gifts and then depart from the rule the giver had in view, whereas in Christ the divine power went on abounding in remedies. Clarke reads the same clause pastorally and widens its scope to as many as were diseased in body or in soul, with the conclusion he wants: where the teaching of Christ is, there also is the power of Christ to redeem and save.

Robertson attends to the vocabulary. The phrase rendered doctors of the law is a compound built on the pattern of another title, and it is one of the very few words that appear to be New Testament coinages, unknown outside the New Testament and the ecclesiastical writers. He adds that there is no word for by in the Greek where the translation has the Pharisees sitting by, and that the tenses through the verse are the periphrastic imperfects Luke favours. Cyril fills in who these listeners were: men who had already been spectators of the miracles, and who now heard him teach as well.
18:
Two of Luke's words are noticed as a physician's. Ellicott points out that the term for the man's condition is more technical than the phrase in the other Gospels — palsy-stricken rather than sick of the palsy — and that the bed let down through the roof is named with a diminutive, a small pallet rather than the bed of the verse before, which is what makes the operation credible. Gill supplies the number of bearers from the parallel, four, and notes that one old version puts it into this text as well.

Whose faith was seen is answered twice. Gill takes it to cover both the sick man and those who carried him, evidenced in the trouble they went to; Chrysostom argues the man's own faith from the manner of it, since he would never have consented to be let down through a roof unless he had believed. Robertson observes that all three Gospels have the same phrase about their faith, that Luke alone addresses the man simply as Man where the others say child or son, and that Luke's form of the verb for forgiven is an old Doric perfect where the others have a present. He adds that this man's malady may have been the consequence of his sin, as sometimes happens.

The objection the scribes make silently is turned back on them by argument. Clarke grants their premise: if Jesus were not God he could not forgive sins, and to claim the authority would be blasphemy in the strictest sense — which is why, he says, three miracles are worked in their presence, each possible only to one omniscient and omnipotent. Ambrose makes the first of the three decisive: the Lord shows himself God by knowing their secret thoughts. Cyril sharpens it into a reply in their own terms: since you say that none but God can forgive sins, answer me who but God can search the secrets of the heart — he who says by the prophet that he is the Lord who searches the hearts and tries the reins. Chrysostom gives the sequence as an argument in stages: if you disbelieve the forgiveness, here is a second thing, that I lay open your inmost thoughts, and a third, that I make the palsied body whole.

Augustine reads the word of forgiveness as doing two things at once. That the man had his sins forgiven follows from his being a man, since no man can say he has not sinned; and that the one forgiving them should be recognised as God follows from the forgiving itself.

Chrysostom draws the practical lesson from the order of the cure. When we suffer in the body we take trouble enough to be rid of what hurts us, but when the harm has fallen on the soul we delay — and so, he says, we are not cured of the bodily ailment either. Remove the fountain of the evil and the waters of sickness stop flowing.

Robertson finds in the narrative itself a piece of evidence about the Gospels. The aside naming the man Jesus is speaking to interrupts his words at exactly the same point in all three accounts, which Robertson takes as conclusive proof that the three documents stand in some relation to one another.

On the ending, Ellicott catches something only Luke reports: the healed man glorified God himself, and not only the bystanders. Robertson notes the imperfect in the phrase about the bed, the thing on which he had been lying. Gill limits the crowd that glorified God to the common people rather than the Pharisees and doctors. And Clarke stops on the word for what they had seen, which means paradoxes — things that look false or absurd, or run contrary to received opinion; we should have concluded these were tricks, he says, were it not for the indisputable evidence of their reality.
27:
Henry frames the whole section before it begins. What follows is not a miracle in nature but an account of the wonders of his grace — which, he says, are no less cogent proofs that Christ was sent of God, to anyone who understands things rightly. That poor fishermen were admitted to the honour of discipleship was condescension enough; that a publican should be called from the receipt of custom is a further wonder still.

The double name is explained by three of the witnesses in the same direction. Augustine identifies the publican Levi with Matthew without argument. Robertson notes that the other accounts add the son of Alphaeus and call him Matthew, and concludes simply that he had both names, adding that all three Gospels use the same phrase for the toll-place and all three record the same two words of command. Bede reads the divergence as a courtesy with a purpose: Luke and Mark decline to attach the common name to a fellow evangelist, while Matthew in his own book is the first to accuse himself, setting down Matthew and publican together — so that no one should despair of salvation on account of the greatness of his sins, when the writer himself had been changed from a tax-collector into an apostle.

Lightfoot supplies what the toll-booth was called in the rabbinic schools, the house of tribute, and quotes a parable that turns on it: the matter is like a king of flesh and blood passing by the house of tribute, who says to his servants, pay the tax to the publicans. Gill fills in the movement, the walk out of the town to the lake side after the morning's dispute — not only for rest, he thinks, but in order to meet the man who was to be called.

What the leaving cost is made much of. Robertson points out that the detail about forsaking all belongs to Luke alone, and that the man left a profitable business to do it. Clarke presses the completeness of it — the office abandoned and everything connected with it — and turns the example on the ministry: a man who wishes to preach as the disciples did must have no earthly entanglement, since one will mar the whole of his labour, the concerns of his own soul and of those he preaches to being enough to engross all his powers. Ellicott catches a tense that extends the act beyond the moment: he followed him not then only but continually, the verb being an imperfect.

The feast raises a question of timing which Gill answers by common sense. It can hardly have been held the same day, since so large an entertainment could not have been got ready in the time; it is recorded here but probably took place later. Gill also reads Levi's motive twice over. The man was evidently rich, and made the feast in gratitude for the grace and honour done him; but he seems to have had a second purpose, to bring Christ into the company of his fellow publicans in the hope that he might be as useful to them as he had been to him. That, Gill adds, is the nature of true grace — to want the salvation of other men's souls as well as one's own.

Barnes closes the section on a point about the sources rather than the supper. This circumstance is missing from the account written by the man who gave the feast, who does not mention his own hospitality at all.
30:
Who exactly complained, and to whom, is worked out carefully. Gill takes the scribes named here to be those of the nation at large rather than any belonging to the company at table, and notes that the eastern versions drop the possessive altogether. Robertson keeps it and makes it the point: the Greek does not say scribes and Pharisees but the Pharisees and the scribes belonging to them, with the article before each, though some manuscripts omit the pronoun. Ellicott observes that the verb is better given as were murmuring, and adds a small point about reporting: in setting down what other men said, Luke naturally keeps their word sinners as they actually spoke it.

Augustine notices that Luke has aimed the objection differently from the other two accounts. Here it is not put to the Lord alone but to the disciples as well, so that the charge is to be understood of both together; where the other evangelists have it made to the disciples about him.

Ambrose does not treat the question as a question at all. It was the voice of the Devil, he says, and the first word the Serpent spoke to Eve was of the same kind — asking whether God had really said they were not to eat. Those who ask such things are diffusing their father's poison.

Gill notes what the reply concedes about the aim of the complaint. Although in this account the objectors named only the disciples, Jesus knew the charge was meant for him, and so took the cause up and vindicated them both at once.

The proverb he answers with contains, on two readings, another trace of the man writing it down. Ellicott points out that where the other Gospels use a word strictly meaning those who are strong, Luke uses the word for those who are in health, which he counts as characteristic of the physician. Robertson identifies the same word as the ordinary Greek term for good health, sound in body, and notes that Luke uses it elsewhere as well.

Gill takes the two halves of the saying as describing two settled conditions rather than two moods. The righteous are such as the scribes and Pharisees were in their own estimate and in other men's — men who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and would not submit to the righteousness of Christ, and whom he therefore did not seek out. The sinners are the company Levi had gathered; and Gill presses the last word of the verse, that Christ did not merely summon them to repentance by the outward ministry of the word but brought them to it, having power to bestow the grace of repentance as well as to call men to the duty of it.
33:
Cyril reads the second objection as a tactic. Having been answered once, the questioners move on to something else, meaning to show that the disciples and their master alike thought very little of the law. He puts their reasoning into their own mouths: you eat with publicans and sinners, though the law forbids fellowship with the unclean, and compassion is brought in to excuse the transgression; very well, then why do you not at least fast, as men do who mean to live by the law?

His answer turns on what fasting is for. Holy men fast so that by mortifying the body they may put down its passions; Christ had no need of it for the perfecting of virtue, being as God free of every yoke of passion, and his companions none either, since they were made partakers of his grace without it. Cyril anticipates the objection that Christ did fast forty days, and answers that this was not to subdue passions of his own but to set out the rule of abstinence for carnal men.

Robertson notices how much of the complaint belongs to Luke alone. The word for fasting often and the phrase about making supplications are both his; and the critics here are the disciples of John and the Pharisees appearing together, though Luke does not press the contrast as the other accounts do. He adds a suggestion that would give the exchange its edge — that Levi's reception may have fallen on one of the Jewish fast days. Wesley glosses the prayers as long and solemn ones. Augustine has to reconcile the reporting: Luke gives the question as put by others about the disciples, where the parallel has the disciples of John asking on their own behalf; he supposes that they too came, everyone pressing the question as far as he could.

Augustine also supplies the distinction that organises the reply. There are two fasts, he says: one of tribulation, undertaken to propitiate God for sin, and one of joy, when carnal things please us less and we feed the more on spiritual ones. The Lord, asked why his disciples did not fast, answers with respect to each in turn — and the words about the bridegroom deal with the first.

The wedding image is unfolded by two of the older readers. Chrysostom states it plainly: the present is a time of joy and gladness, and sorrow is not to be mixed into it. Cyril makes the appearing of the Saviour a great festival, in which our nature is joined to him as a bride so that she who was barren may bear; and on that reading the children of the Bridegroom are those called under a new and evangelical discipline, not the scribes and Pharisees, who keep only the shadow of the law. Augustine finds a darker point in the clause Luke alone records, that these children cannot be made to fast: the men who could not make them fast now were the very men who would make them mourn soon enough, since they were about to kill the Bridegroom.

The form of the reply is noticed by the close readers. Ellicott points out that Luke's question is put more strongly than the plain form in the other reports, which ask only whether the children of the bridechamber can fast. Robertson identifies the difference precisely: Luke adds a verb of making, so that the question is whether one can make them fast, while all three frame it so as to expect the answer no. On the days that are coming, the three accounts diverge in a small way Robertson records — Luke has then in those days, one parallel has then in that day, and the other simply then. Gill adds only what the phrase proved to mean, that the days came, and came very shortly.
36:
Luke alone calls what follows a parable, and both close readers make something of it. Ellicott observes that the illustration is common to all three reports but that only Luke gives it that name, the others apparently reserving the word for something told as an actual narrative. Robertson counts three such illustrations in the answer — the bridegroom, the patch and the wineskin — and says that although nowhere else called parables, they are parables, and Luke's word means exactly that.

The better text of the first one is sharper than the familiar rendering. Ellicott reports the reading in which no man tears a piece out of a new garment to put it on an old one, and points out how much more vivid the folly becomes when stated that way; the second clause then runs that he will both rend the new and find that the patch taken from it does not match the old. Robertson notes that the verb for the tearing is Luke's alone, that it is the ordinary word for splitting a thing — used of rocks broken open — and that our word schism descends from it; on the verb for applying the patch he finds Luke agreeing with one parallel and differing from the other, which says sewing on.

The wineskins are explained from the material. Clarke reminds the reader that eastern bottles are made of skins, generally goat-skins, and that an old one could not stand the fermentation, its old stitching being likely to give way. Ellicott corrects two small things in the English, preferring if otherwise to else, and objecting that the two verbs are rendered differently when there is no reason for any difference between them. Robertson finds in the next verse a form that appears nowhere else in the New Testament though it is common enough in Attic — a survival, he says, of the literary style.

Gill assigns the two kinds of vessel. The old bottles are the scribes and Pharisees, into whose hearts the new wine of gospel grace was never put, and to whom the blessings of the new covenant were not made known; the new ones are the disciples and the sinners called to repentance, renewed by the Spirit and filled with a spiritual gladness that Gill compares to new wine.

Ambrose takes the old garment as fasting itself, and finds his warrant in the apostolic phrase about putting off the old man with his deeds; the string of sayings amounts, on his reading, to a series of precepts against mixing the actions of the old man with those of the new. Augustine reads the same sequence through his distinction between the two kinds of fasting, and locates in the gift of the Spirit a fast of joy belonging to those who are already renewed.

The last saying is the hardest, and it is handled two ways. Lightfoot recovers what old wine meant in the schools: three years old, or, in the phrase the rabbinic note uses, wine of three leaves, because the vine that produced it had put out its leaves three times since. Barnes explains the proverb from the taste itself — wine gains strength and flavour and mellowness with age, and a man who has drunk that will not readily go back to the sharp juice as it comes from the press — and then applies it to the dispute. The Pharisees are trying to draw the disciples to the austere and rigid duties of the ceremonial law, while the disciples have come under a milder system and have tasted its gentleness; to press the sterner requirements on them now would be to offer sour wine to men who have had good. Barnes is careful to add what the proverb does not say: that at the proper time the sterner duties of religion will have their place.
